entry.title: Hot Stove Edition — the Twelfth of November, Two Thousand and Twenty-Six
entry.content:
Is it spring training yet? Not yet — 132 days until Opening Night of the 2027 season — the first pitch of the new campaign, the clubs yet to be named.

THE MORNING HORSEHIDE HERALD

"Every Score Set Down, No Deed Unsung"

~ Being a Faithful Daily Chronicle of the National Pastime ~

Volume I · No. 127 · Thursday, the Twelfth of November, Two Thousand and Twenty-Six

No contests this day; the hot stove burns bright.

132 days until Opening Night of the 2027 season — the first pitch of the new campaign, the clubs yet to be named (Wednesday, the 24th of March, 2027).

News Around the League

THE LAURELS DESK: SIXTY BALLOTS, SIXTY FIRSTS — MISIOROWSKI OF THE MILWAUKEES AND SCHLITTLER OF THE BRONX TAKE THE CY YOUNGS WITHOUT A SINGLE DISSENTING PEN, A DOUBLE UNANIMITY SEEN BUT TWICE BEFORE IN ALL THE AWARD'S HISTORY, AND THE WRITERS CROWN THEIR FIRST RELIEVERS BESIDES

The writers did not deliberate so much as transcribe. The Baseball Writers' Association of America read its Cy Young verdicts Wednesday night on the MLB Network — Roger Clemens, seven times the award's owner, opening both envelopes — and Jacob Misiorowski of the champion Brewers and Cam Schlittler of the Yankees were named on all 30 ballots apiece, first place on every one, 210 points a man. Two leagues unanimous in the same November is a thing the award has produced only twice before: Justin Verlander and Sandy Alcantara in 2022, and Denny McLain and Bob Gibson in the year of the pitcher itself, 1968. The reader of Monday's columns will recall that MLB.com's September poll of its own scribes called both races exactly so, and that this paper printed the result under its standing caution that a poll is a poll; the only electorate that counts has now ratified the straw vote to the last pen.243

The National League's trophy goes to the fastest arm the game has ever timed in a starting pitcher. Misiorowski, 24, led all the Majors in earned-run average at 1.80, in strikeouts with 252, in WHIP at 0.80 and in opponents' batting average at .157 — the lowest full-season figure on record, beneath even Pedro Martínez's .167 of 2000 — across 174 and two-thirds innings in 30 starts, and he did it throwing a four-seamer that averaged 100.6 mph and once reached 105.5, a record for a man in a rotation. Since 1950 only Sandy Koufax in 1965, J.R. Richard in 1979 and Mike Scott in 1986 had led the Majors in earned-run average, strikeouts and opponents' average together.2 He is the fourth Milwaukee man to take the award, after Rollie Fingers, Pete Vuckovich and Corbin Burnes, and the first to pair it with a World Series ring in the same autumn. The hero's own account of life since the parade runs to hunting with his father and a football game. "It's an honor to represent my city and my teammates," he said. "Just being in this situation is awesome."2

The American League's goes to the seventh-round pick who out-pitched every first-rounder alive. Schlittler, 25, taken in the seventh round out of Northeastern in 2022, led his league in earned-run average at 1.95 — the third-best by a Yankee qualifier in all the franchise's books, behind only Spud Chandler's 1.64 of 1943 and Ron Guidry's 1.74 of 1978 — and in opponents' on-base percentage at .244, this for a club that reached October with Aaron Judge long absent and three veteran starters short of 130 innings. The road ledger is the historical marvel: a 1.16 earned-run average away from home, the third-lowest of the live-ball era for a man with 100 road innings, behind only Gibson's 0.81 of 1968 and Greg Maddux's 1.12 of 1995.2 He is the seventh Yankee winner, after Turley, Ford, Lyle, Guidry, Clemens and Cole. "Surreal to be in this moment," he said, and then, with the champion Brewers evidently in mind: "The job isn't done yet."2

The margins behind the unanimity deserve their line in the ledger. In the National League, Cristopher Sánchez of the Phillies took second with 99 points and Chris Sale of the Braves third with 98 — a single point between them — while in the American, Dylan Cease of the Torontos stood second at 110, the rookie Parker Messick of Cleveland third at 84 and Drew Rasmussen of the Tampa men fourth at 72.3 Both winners claimed the prize in their second big-league season, a feat managed before only by Fernando Valenzuela (who did it as a rookie in 1981), by Gooden and Saberhagen sharing the stage in 1985, by Tim Lincecum in 2008, and by Paul Skenes only last year.2 The same sitting produced the writers' first Reliever of the Year honors, inaugurated this winter: Louis Varland of the Torontos in the American League, on a 1.27 earned-run average and 35 saves across 78 innings, and Mason Miller of the San Diego nine in the National — names the reader will meet again one item below, where the matter grows complicated.26

THE THEATER OF SILVER: THE LEAGUE STAGES ITS REVUE AT LAS VEGAS — ALVAREZ CARRIES THREE PRIZES FROM A SINGLE EVENING, THE AARON AWARDS GO TO THE TWO MEN FAVORED FOR TONIGHT'S VERDICTS, AND THE TWO HOUSES OF RELIEF AGREE ON ONE ARM AND SPLIT ON THE OTHER

While the writers read their ballots, the league threw its party. The MLB Awards played Wednesday night at the Chelsea Theater of the Cosmopolitan at Las Vegas, Mookie Betts and the comedian Roy Wood Jr. presiding for a second year — the hosts ran their jokes through their own version of the automated strike zone, to rule each one in or out of the joke zone — and the Hank Aaron Awards for the finest offensive performers went to Yordan Alvarez of the Houston nine and Pete Crow-Armstrong of the Cubs, with Ken Griffey Jr., the 2006 winner Ryan Howard and Mrs. Billye Aaron presenting. The pair arrive at tonight's Most Valuable announcements as the favorites, by the wire's reckoning, and the theater may thus have given the week's last secret a loud hint.5

Alvarez made the evening nearly his own. To the Aaron award he added the Edgar Martínez prize for the game's outstanding designated hitter — unseating Ohtani, the award's first new winner in six years — and the American League's Comeback Player honor besides, three trophies in one sitting for a season of .316, a .432 on-base mark, 42 home runs and 106 driven in, the league led in average, on-base, slugging and OPS alike. "Especially because I wear the No. 44," he said, naming the number he shares with Aaron. "It's very special for me to see my name on this award." Zack Wheeler of the Phillies took the National League's comeback honor.5

And the relief question this paper posed on Monday — whether the writers' new electors and the panel of old closers who award the Rivera and Hoffman medals could agree on the same arms — has its answer: in one league yes, in the other no. The National League spoke with one voice, the Trevor Hoffman Award going to Mason Miller of the San Diego nine, the same man the writers chose: a 1.67 earned-run average, the best among the league's qualified relievers, with 129 strikeouts in 70 innings — a 47.4 percent strikeout rate, the highest for any pitcher with 50 innings since Edwin Díaz in 2022 — on a fastball averaging 101.4 mph. He is the first Padre ever to win the medal struck in a Padre's name. The American League split its houses: the writers chose Varland, as the columns above record, while the panel gave the Mariano Rivera Award to Bryan Baker of the Tampa men, whose 41 saves tied Cleveland's Cade Smith for the most in the Majors and whose 1.44 earned-run average stood second among qualified relievers only to Varland himself — and who then went unscored upon through nine October appearances while his club took the pennant. The Herald, which keeps its subscriptions for exactly such disagreements, is satisfied on both counts.65

The night's remaining silver, briskly: Erik Neander of the Tampa men was voted Executive of the Year by his fellow executives, his second such honor, joining Matt Arnold of Milwaukee — whose club beat his in the World Series — as the award's only two-time winners. "Arnie, you were up here a year ago accepting this trophy and cashed it in for a championship," Neander said. "I can't believe I'm saying this — but I've never wanted to be you more." William Contreras, Most Valuable of the late Series, received the first Flow Mayor Award for style and self-expression, presented with a diamond-studded toothpick by his brother Willson; Colton Cowser's game-ending robbery of a home run was named the Premier Play of the Year; and the All-MLB First Team was read, its rotation — Misiorowski, Schlittler, Sale, Cease and Sánchez — amounting to the two Cy Young winners, the two runners-up and the National League's third man, with Miller and Varland its bullpen.5

THE DUGOUT DESK: HOUSTON CALLS ITS OLD CATCHER HOME — AUSMUS, SEVEN-AND-FIFTY, WHO CAUGHT MORE GAMES FOR THE CLUB THAN ANY MAN IN ITS BOOKS, LEAVES THE YANKEE COACHING ROOMS TO TAKE THE CHAIR LATELY ESPADA'S

The managerial carousel, which has turned all autumn, stopped Wednesday at a familiar face. The Astros named Brad Ausmus their manager, the club announced, with a formal introduction set for Friday at Daikin Park — and the appointment reads less like a hiring than a homecoming. Ausmus, 57, caught more games for Houston than any man in the franchise's history across two tours totaling 10 of his 18 playing seasons, won three Gold Gloves in the uniform, and caught the pitching staffs of the 1997 and 1998 division winners and the 2005 pennant club; his two-out, game-tying home run in the ninth inning of the 2005 Division Series' fourth game, ahead of Chris Burke's winner in the 18th, remains among the franchise's treasured strokes.7

The chair comes with a record already written. Ausmus managed five seasons before this engagement — the Tigers from 2014 through 2017, with a division title in his first year and 86 wins in his third, and the Angels of 2019 — to a combined 386-422, and spent the last three years as bench coach of the Yankees, whose own newly laureled ace the reader met two items above. He succeeds Joe Espada, whose contract was not renewed after three seasons and two division flags, and he arrives a fortnight behind the man who hired him: Randy Flores, whose removal from St. Louis to the head of Houston's baseball operations these columns chronicled last week, and whose Cardinals fought Ausmus's Astros through back-to-back league championship series as the two men played against each other in 2004 and 2005. The senior advisor Jeff Bagwell, Ausmus's teammate across both Houston tours, sat in on the hiring.7

"The Astros and the City of Houston have been a huge part of my life," the new manager said, "and I'm thrilled to create a new chapter as the team's manager." Flores pronounced himself "excited to work alongside Brad and happy to have him back in an Astros uniform." The work begins at once: a bench coach must be found, the club having parted with five members of the late staff, and a roster that was swept from October's opening round awaits instruction. The Herald observes that Houston has now restocked its front office and its dugout inside a single month, and that the winter's remaining question — the roster itself — is the one neither man can answer by introduction alone.7

THE INK DESK: THE POTOMAC NINE BUY FOUR YEARS OF THE FINEST GLOVE IN THEIR GARDEN — YOUNG, SEVEN-AND-TWENTY, SIGNS THROUGH 2030 WITH AN OPTION BESIDES, A WAGER ON LEATHER LAID DOWN WITH THE AGREEMENT'S EXPIRY IN PLAIN VIEW

The week's quietest signature may prove its most telling. The Nationals agreed to terms with their center fielder Jacob Young on a contract running four years through the 2030 season, with a club option for 2031, the president of baseball operations Paul Toboni announced Wednesday from the meetings at Las Vegas. Young, who turned 27 in late July, is a defense-first outfielder by anyone's ledger — third among the National League's center fielders this season in outs above average and in runs prevented, and a Gold Glove finalist in both 2024 and 2025 — whose bat has lately begun to answer: a .252 average with career highs of 10 home runs and 50 runs driven in, this from a man who had brought 5 home runs to the season in his first 1,006 big-league plate appearances.8

"Already one of the top defenders in Major League Baseball, we all saw the significant step forward Jacob took offensively in 2026," Toboni said, "and we anticipate continued development in the years to come." The timing is its own commentary: the ink dries 19 mornings before the collective agreement expires on the 1st of December, with the industry braced for the freeze these columns have charted all week — a club locking in its young glove while the locking-in can still be done. The Herald notes with approval that somebody in the capital is planning for 2031 while the rest of the sport cannot say with certainty what happens on the 2nd of December.8

THE EXCHANGE DESK: THE SUITORS' REGISTER LENGTHENS — THE TORONTOS BOOK THEIR OWN AUDIENCE WITH SKUBAL, THE YANKEES EYE BOHM FOR THE HOT CORNER, AND THE DESERT FRONT OFFICE OPENS THE MARTE QUESTION A SECOND WINTER RUNNING

The Skubal sweepstakes, which yesterday's columns left with the Mets booking passage to California, added a fourth confirmed suitor Wednesday: the Blue Jays will soon take their own meeting with the left-hander, joining the Mets, Dodgers and Padres in the audience chamber of the agent Scott Boras. The Toronto case writes itself in recent ink — a $500 million extension for Guerrero, $210 million for Dylan Cease — and the trade now talks of an annual wage in the neighborhood of $45 million, comfortably past the $43.3 million record Scherzer and Verlander share. The complication is arithmetic: the Torontos scored the fewest runs in all baseball this past season, and a purse emptied into one arm is a purse unavailable for bats, with the free outfielder Seiya Suzuki reckoned the market's neatest fit for their order. Pitching or hitting, but perhaps not both; it is the oldest sentence in the winter's grammar.9

In the Bronx, the shopping list runs to the infield. The Yankees have interest in Alec Bohm, seven years a Phillie and lately a free agent, as a right-handed partner for the left-swinging Ryan McMahon at third base — a station that gave New York a .629 OPS this season, 26th in the game. Bohm's own year ran crooked: a miserable first half dragged his line to .698, but he posted .794 after the All-Star interval, and his career-long habits — little given to the walk but little given to the strikeout either, his career strikeout rate of 17 percent sitting well under the league's 22, with an .853 OPS against left-handed pitching — describe exactly the platoon hand the Yankee ledger wants. The Post's reporting has him likely signing short, perhaps a single year, which suits a club that prefers its commitments at third base brief.10

And in Arizona, a name this paper listed Monday among those to be spoken of "chiefly by men who do not employ them" is now being spoken of by the men who do. The general manager Mike Hazen, three straight autumns short of October with the core that reached the 2023 World Series, allows that he must "be open to making adjustments to what the roster looks like" — and the roster's most valuable adjustable part remains Ketel Marte, owed a reasonable $87.5 million over five seasons but armed now with the ten-and-five rights that let him veto any destination, and trailing an August unexcused absence at Boston that obliges the Snakes to ask less than they once might have. The payroll, north of $200 million last season, is to come down; the middle relief has walked off in free agency; and Hazen says the Marte question must settle before the rest of the winter can be planned. The desert's offseason, in short, begins where last winter's ended — with the telephone ringing about the second baseman.11

A Thursday that all but closes the silver season. The Cy Youngs are read without a dissenting pen, the league's theater has struck its set at Las Vegas, and one envelope remains: the Most Valuable verdicts are announced this evening, closing the week's long bill exactly as Monday's columns scheduled it, with the Aaron-award pair of Alvarez and Crow-Armstrong installed as the favorites by the wire.5 The courtroom at Brooklyn resumes its proceedings this very day, as Monday's columns also noted. The forward ledger was ruled open before a word was set, per the house custom, and it reads as it has read all week: the next baseball on the card is the spring exhibition slate of Friday, the 19th of February — 99 mornings from this one — with Opening Night to follow 132 mornings off, on Wednesday, the 24th of March.1 The 17th keeps its double appointment five mornings hence, qualifying answers and silver bats together, and the collective agreement has 19 mornings left to live — a deadline the week's quietest signature already answers to, as the ink desk above attests. Until the morrow's dispatch, keep your scorecards near and your enthusiasms nearer.

~ THE HERALD ~

entry.content:
Is it spring training yet? Not yet — 133 days until Opening Night of the 2027 season — the first pitch of the new campaign, the clubs yet to be named.

THE MORNING HORSEHIDE HERALD

"Every Score Set Down, No Deed Unsung"

~ Being a Faithful Daily Chronicle of the National Pastime ~

Volume I · No. 126 · Wednesday, the Eleventh of November, Two Thousand and Twenty-Six

No contests this day; the hot stove burns bright.

133 days until Opening Night of the 2027 season — the first pitch of the new campaign, the clubs yet to be named (Wednesday, the 24th of March, 2027).

News Around the League

THE LAURELS DESK: THRICE RUNNING — MURPHY OF THE CREAM CITY NINE TAKES THE MANAGERS' PRIZE AS NO MAN BEFORE HIM EVER HAS, AND HEARS THE NEWS FROM A HOSPITAL BED, WHILE VENABLE OF THE SOUTH SIDERS, TWO AUTUMNS REMOVED FROM A HUNDRED AND TWENTY-ONE DEFEATS, CARRIES OFF THE AMERICAN HONOR

Pat Murphy took the call of history lying down, and no man alive has better earned the posture. The Baseball Writers' Association of America read its Managers of the Year on Tuesday evening, and the National League's went where yesterday's columns weighed it: to the 67-year-old steward of the champion Brewers, who thereby becomes the first manager in either league ever to win the award three years in succession — a thing only four men had done even twice running. Murphy, who underwent back surgery in June and has lately had a hip replaced besides, accepted the honor over the television wire from a hospital bed. "I'm really grateful," he said. "I don't necessarily think I'm deserving, to be quite honest with you. It's more a matter of just keeping everything in perspective, but I'm super, super grateful." The writers suffered no such modesty: he was named on all 30 ballots — 20 firsts, seven seconds, three thirds, 124 points — with Walt Weiss of the Atlantas second at 86 and Don Mattingly of the Phillies third at 25, a single point ahead of the Friars' Craig Stammen. Murphy joins the register as the tenth manager with three such awards or more; Buck Showalter, Bobby Cox and Tony La Russa head that table with four apiece, but no collection among the ten came three Novembers running — that distinction is now Murphy's alone. The campaign beneath the trophy wants no restating: 103 victories, the best in all the game for a second consecutive year, and then the 11-2 October march that ended in the franchise's first championship.23

The American League's prize went to the resurrection man. Will Venable, who inherited a White Sox club fresh from the 121 defeats of 2024 — the most any modern nine had ever suffered — was named on 15 first-place ballots and totaled 111 points, holding off Kevin Cash of the Rays at 98 and Boston's mid-season inheritor Chad Tracy at 47, whose father-and-son particular must now wait upon some other November. In Venable's first year the South Siders improved by 19 games and still lost 102; in his second they won 84, took the league's final Wild Card berth, swept Houston from the opening round, and won the first two games of the Division Series at Cleveland before the Guardians came back for the set. He is the club's first Manager of the Year since Ozzie Guillén in the championship season of 2005, a son of the old big-leaguer Max Venable, and himself nine years an outfielder for the Padres, Rangers and Dodgers before the coaching rooms of Chicago and Boston raised him to a chair of his own. He declined, characteristically, to sit in it alone: "You can have the best front office, the best staff; you can support them the best you can. At the end of the day, it's about getting guys that want to go and compete, so I think it really starts with the players." Of the spring that started it: "This group in Spring Training developed a belief in themselves, a belief in each other, and then went out and did it."2

The evening carried a coda from the gracious side of the ledger. When the champagne flew on the 28th of October, a live microphone caught Murphy — handed the final-out ball by Jake Bauers — urging his first baseman to remember his old club, the 2023 Yankees of the selfish reputation, with a profanity attached. Within half a day, by Brian Cashman's own telling, Murphy had tracked down "the lowly New York Yankees" at their offices to say he regretted it. "He took the time on the greatest — within 12 hours, arguably some of the greatest times that he's had walking this planet Earth outside of the birth of his kids — to realize that he said something that he regretted," the Yankee general manager said Tuesday at Las Vegas. "That meant a lot to me." Murphy called Cashman "very gracious and very, very kind," and offered this by way of explanation: "I could have said the Dodgers or the Giants or whoever." The Herald files the exchange under manners, a department the sport does not always keep staffed, and notes that the week's silver bill is only half discharged: the Cy Youngs and the writers' first reliever's prize are read this very evening, with the Most Valuable verdicts to close the books on the morrow.4

THE HERALD LOWERS ITS COLORS: BOB BOONE, CATCHER OF THE QUAKERS' FIRST CHAMPIONSHIP AND MIDDLE LINK OF THE GAME'S FIRST THREE-GENERATION HOUSE, IS DEAD AT EIGHT-AND-SEVENTY — SEVEN GOLD GLOVES, MORE THAN TWO THOUSAND GAMES BEHIND THE PLATE, AND A NAME THE SPORT STILL ANSWERS TO

The game has lost the man in the middle of its first dynasty of blood. Bob Boone, catcher of the Phillies' first World Series championship and patriarch-in-the-middle of baseball's first three-generation family, is dead at 78; his son Bret announced the passing on Tuesday, and no cause was given. "He was a man of great integrity. He was a great dad, husband, and patriarch. It was a privilege to call him my father," Bret wrote. "Baseball lost a great one today."5

The playing ledger is a monument to endurance at the game's most punishing station. Drafted out of Stanford in 1969 as a third baseman and converted behind the plate in the minors, Boone caught for 19 big-league seasons — ten with Philadelphia, seven with the Angels of California, two with Kansas City — and his 2,225 games caught stood as the record in their day, since passed only by Carlton Fisk and Iván Rodríguez. He won seven Gold Gloves, the last of them at 41; made three All-Star teams; and in the October of 1980 led the Phillies at .412 as they beat the Royals for the franchise's first title, catching the final strike when Tug McGraw fanned Willie Wilson. Moments earlier in that same inning came the play Philadelphia never tires of re-running: Frank White's foul pop glancing off Boone's mitt by the dugout and dropping, as if by appointment, into Pete Rose's glove. He later managed both the Royals and the Reds, and the Phillies set him on their Wall of Fame in 2005. "We played in the minors together where he gave up third base so I could play it, only to become one of the best catchers in baseball history," said Mike Schmidt, his teammate of a decade. "We lost a close friend."5

And then there is the house itself. His father, Ray Boone, played 13 seasons and twice made the All-Star team for Detroit; his son Bret was three times an All-Star across 14 years spent largely in Seattle; his son Aaron played 13 seasons — some of them in Cincinnati under his father's management — and today manages the Yankees, who mourned "an exceptional player, respected manager and distinguished executive" and said they see his values carried forward in their own dugout; a grandson, Jake, works in the Mets' front office. Four generations in the game's employ, and the second of them its sturdiest hinge. The Herald lowers its colors for a man who squatted behind the plate past his fortieth birthday and never once made durability look like drudgery — the game asked him to catch, and for the better part of three decades, in one capacity or another, he never stopped.5

THE EXCHANGE DESK: THE SUITORS BOOK PASSAGE TO CALIFORNIA — THE METS WILL SIT WITH SKUBAL HIMSELF NEXT WEEK AND THE DODGERS BESIDES, THE ATLANTAS PRONOUNCE THEIR RIGHT FIELDER NOT FOR SALE WITH SOME HEAT, AND SEATTLE PARTS WITH THE LAST MAN OF ITS REBUILDING

The winter's great sweepstakes advanced from corridor talk to calendar entries on Tuesday. The Mets — installed by the trade as the favorites for Tarik Skubal only yesterday morning in these columns — will fly officials to Los Angeles next week to meet the left-hander and his representatives, and the Dodgers' general manager Brandon Gomes allowed that his club, which rented Skubal's summer services at the cost of three prospects, will take its own meeting. David Stearns declined all comment on the man himself but took direct aim at the theory that he will not pay long for pitching: "Every situation is unique, and it's been also well publicized even since I've been here — we've engaged in extremely long-term negotiations for pitchers and we will do so again. But situation matters." What he would commit to is appetite: "There's no question we're going to add to that group." The object of all this scheduling turns 30 next week and owns, over the past four seasons, a record of 50-20, an earned-run average of 2.47 and the best league-adjusted pitching figure in the game among arms with 300 innings — against which stands the surgeon's ledger, multiple elbow operations since 2023 and a career high of just 195 and one-third innings. The trade still expects him to sail past the $325 million that Yoshinobu Yamamoto's contract presently marks as the water line; whether Stearns, whose richest pitching deal in Queens remains Sean Manaea's three years and $75 million, or his owner's famous purse writes the number is the question the Aria's corridors chew on.6

At Atlanta's table the general manager spent his Tuesday stamping out a fire he insists was never lit. Asked about the speculation that Ronald Acuña Jr. might be moved — talk fed by a miserable October of 3 hits in 24 at-bats, boos at home, and the outfielder wiping the club from his Instagram — Alex Anthopoulos went to the record with unusual relish: "There's not even a hint of smoke to it. There's zero... There have been zero conversations. And I don't mind saying that on the record. Zero. None. No phone calls. Incoming, outgoing." The origin he assigned the rumor — "somebody on his computer, in his basement, put it out there" — is the nearest thing to period invective the meetings have yet produced. Acuña, who turns 29 next month and batted .255 with 20 home runs across an injury-shortened 107 games, had his $17 million option for 2027 exercised the moment the World Series ended. "He's a huge part of our club," Anthopoulos said. "We need him. We need to add to him."7

And in the northwest, an era was shown the door with honors. The Mariners have informed J.P. Crawford, their shortstop of eight seasons and the longest-serving man on the roster, that they do not intend to bring him back — this though Crawford said as recently as May, "I want to be a Mariner for life." He is 31, a free agent for the first time after playing out five years and $51 million, and the last man standing from the club's first true rebuilding; on the season's final day the Puget Sound men pulled him for a defensive replacement so the park could stand and cheer, and the man wept where he stood. The succession is its own winter's work: young Colt Emerson, extended for $95 million in the spring, is the heir presumptive at shortstop but comes off a rookie year wrecked by a wrist that wanted surgery, and the club's whole left-handed lineup wants right-handed ballast besides, with Randy Arozarena expected to decline his qualifying tender and test the water. The Herald observes that rebuildings are usually reckoned by the stars they produce, and that this one may be best reckoned by the complementary piece who became its conscience.8

THE INFIRMARY WARD: THE PINSTRIPES' LEFT ARM IS SWEPT CLEAN OF ITS SPUR AND PROMISED FOR THE SPRING — THE CAPTAIN'S RIB KNITS WITHOUT FURTHER SURGERY, AND BROWN OF THE NORTH SIDERS TAKES A SCREW IN THE NECK AND AN APPOINTMENT WITH THE NEW YEAR

The surgeons' week continues brisk. In New York, Max Fried has had a bone spur removed from his pitching elbow — the joint whose "bone bruise" twice sent him to the shelf this past season, in May and again in August — and the Pinstripes expect their left-hander ready for the spring, whose first exhibitions are listed for February 19.91 Fried, who turns 33 in January and enters the third year of his eight-year, $218 million engagement, posted a 2.80 earned-run average across 20 starts when the elbow permitted; Brian Cashman set the protocol at six weeks of rest before a training program begins in the second week of December. The same briefing carried the winter's most consequential clean bill: Aaron Judge's fractured rib, reviewed by the specialist who has watched over its healing, requires no procedure at all — "He's currently in a good place," Cashman said, prescribing only a winter of rest for the captain whose absence reduced the Yankee attack to 66 games of its best man. "I know one thing — we'll be instantly better if we have a healthy Aaron Judge."9

Chicago's news asks more patience. Ben Brown, the young right-hander whose 1.85 earned-run average over 20 appearances was among the few unqualified pleasures of the North Siders' pitching year, underwent cervical spine surgery Monday in New York — a screw set at the fifth vertebra to stabilize a fracture, the second time in three years his neck has stopped his season. The club expects him throwing early in the new year and game-ready in the first half of 2027. "He's walking around, looks great," said the general manager Carter Hawkins. "We expect to have him back next year." The Herald wishes the young man a dull and uneventful convalescence; a rotation that already buried the seasons of Cade Horton and Justin Steele has earned a little tedium.10

THE INK DESK: THE BENGALS BUY A LATE-INNINGS ARM FOR ELEVEN MILLIONS — PAGÁN CROSSES FROM ONE ROOKIE-LAUREL HOUSE TO THE OTHER, WHILE THE FRIARS, WANTING VERY NEARLY A WHOLE ROTATION, SIGN THE FIRST ARM OF THE MANY THEY WILL NEED

The week's first notable signatures are relievers' and reclamations'. Detroit is in agreement with Emilio Pagán on one year and $11 million, the deal pending a physical — and the clerks note the small symmetry that the club whose rookie took Monday's American laurels has gone shopping in the pen of the club whose rookie took the National. Pagán, who enters his age-36 campaign, spent the past two seasons with Cincinnati pitching to a 3.07 earned-run average across 111 and one-third innings, holding batters to a .185 average over that span, though a hamstring cost him nearly two months of the summer just closed. The fastball still arrives at an average of 94.9 mph, with a cutter beside it; the Bengals, who parted with their twice-laureled ace at midseason and crowned a Rookie of the Year on Monday, have bought themselves some certainty for the eighth inning.11

San Diego's signature is humbler and more telling. The Friars signed the right-hander Ryan Weiss to a Major League contract with a club option for 2028 — a 29-year-old who pitched to a 7.62 earned-run average in nine outings for Houston, was let go to Triple-A Sugar Land, and finished the year there striking out 24 men in his final 19 and two-thirds innings at a 1.37 mark, after two seasons of solid work for the Hanwha Eagles of Korea before that. The context is the point: seven San Diego starters, Michael King, Nick Pivetta and Walker Buehler among them, walked into free agency at the season's end, leaving a rotation of Randy Vásquez and question marks. "You can never have too much, from a starting pitching standpoint," said A.J. Preller, the man now obliged to prove it. "We're going to need multiples." Weiss is the first; the Herald will keep the running count.12

A Wednesday of silver given and silver promised. The managers' prizes are bestowed — one to a hospital bed in Milwaukee, one to the South Side — and the week's bill holds to the schedule this paper printed Monday: the Cy Youngs and the writers' first reliever's prize are read this evening, while the league stages its awards theater at the Chelsea Theater of the Cosmopolitan at Las Vegas at 9 o'clock Eastern, Mookie Betts and the comedian Roy Wood Jr. presiding over the Aaron awards, the reliever medals and the rest of the glitter;13 the Most Valuable verdicts close the books on the morrow, the same day the courtroom at Brooklyn resumes, as Monday's columns noted. The forward ledger, ruled open at first light as the house requires, stands unmoved: nothing on the card before the spring exhibitions of Friday, the 19th of February, 100 mornings from this one, with Opening Night 133 mornings off on Wednesday, the 24th of March.1 The 17th keeps its double appointment six mornings hence — qualifying answers and silver bats together — and the collective agreement has 20 mornings left to live. The desk notes, finally, what the date at the masthead already says: this is the eleventh morning of the eleventh month, Armistice Day by the old reckoning, and a paper set in this type remembers the eleventh hour of 1918 and every man of the game who ever traded flannels for khaki. Until the next dispatch, keep your scorecards near and your enthusiasms nearer.

entry.title: Hot Stove Edition — the Tenth of November, Two Thousand and Twenty-Six
entry.content:
Is it spring training yet? Not yet — 134 days until Opening Night of the 2027 season — the first pitch of the new campaign, the clubs yet to be named.

THE MORNING HORSEHIDE HERALD

"Every Score Set Down, No Deed Unsung"

~ Being a Faithful Daily Chronicle of the National Pastime ~

Volume I · No. 125 · Tuesday, the Tenth of November, Two Thousand and Twenty-Six

No contests this day; the hot stove burns bright.

134 days until Opening Night of the 2027 season — the first pitch of the new campaign, the clubs yet to be named (Wednesday, the 24th of March, 2027).

News Around the League

THE LAURELS DESK: THE ROOKIES' PRIZES GO TO THE EVERYDAY MEN — McGONIGLE OF THE MOTOR CITY NINE TAKES THE AMERICAN HONOR ON EIGHT-AND-TWENTY FIRST-PLACE BALLOTS OF THIRTY, STEWART OF THE QUEEN CITY THE NATIONAL, AND THE CLEVELAND WAIT OUTLIVES ANOTHER NOVEMBER

The first verdicts of the writers' week are opened, and both prizes went to men who never took a day off the argument. The Baseball Writers' Association of America announced Monday evening that Kevin McGonigle, the Tigers' infielder of 22, is the American League's Rookie of the Year, and that Sal Stewart, the Reds' first baseman of the same age, is the National League's — the ballots, the reader is reminded, having been sealed before the postseason began, two writers voting in every city. The American League's two-man argument of the everyday against the every-fifth-day, as yesterday's columns framed it, resolved emphatically for the everyday: McGonigle took 28 of the 30 first-place votes and 204 points, against 122 for the Cleveland left-hander Parker Messick, who collected the other two firsts. The National League's was the more divided sitting, and Stewart won it all the same — 20 first-place votes and 170 points, over the Mets' outfielder Carson Benge (7 firsts, 107 points) and the Cardinals' second baseman JJ Wetherholt (3 firsts, 99).23

The case for McGonigle wanted no advocate. In his age-21 season the young man led the American League outright in plate appearances, with 707, and in Baseball-Reference's wins above replacement, with 7.1 — the first rookie to lead his league by that reckoning since Mike Trout in 2012 — while batting .278 with 18 home runs, 72 runs driven in and 12 stolen bases, and splitting his leather between shortstop and third base to the tune of 10 runs saved. The discipline is the signature: 95 walks against 100 strikeouts, a .376 on-base mark that stood sixth in the league, 97 runs scored, and a place in the top five in both walks and hits that no rookie had claimed since Ted Williams in 1939; since the award was struck in 1947, only Aaron Judge, Joe Morgan and Jim Gilliam had paired 95 walks with 95 runs as first-year men.24 He is the sixth Tiger to win it and the first Detroit position player since Lou Whitaker in 1978. "I don't really know how to put it into words," he said. "I'm just super grateful for how this season went. I worked my butt off to play and help this team win."2

Stewart's ledger reads like a dock manifest. He played all 162 games — "Being available for your teammates every single day — that's something that kind of goes unnoticed at times," he said, naming it his proudest line — stood at three infield stations, and struck 32 home runs, the first National League rookie past 30 since Pete Alonso in 2019 and only the second Reds rookie ever to do it, after Frank Robinson, himself the Rookie of the Year of 1956. His 112 runs driven in, second in the league to Alec Burleson's 116, made him the first Reds rookie and the fourteenth rookie anywhere to pair 30 home runs with 100 runs driven in, and with 15 stolen bases besides he became just the fifth rookie ever to pair 100 runs driven in with 15 steals, after Carlos Beltrán, Jose Canseco, Tony Lazzeri and Al Simmons.24 He is the ninth Cincinnati man to take the award and the second this century, after Jonathan India in 2021. Asked for the feeling, he chose one word: "Relieved. I told myself that this award wouldn't define me. That's how I was raised. I'm excited. I worked hard for this moment. A lot of people doubted me. I'm focused."2

And so the drought columns close unmoved. Messick's candidacy carried Cleveland's 36-year wait to the very threshold — this paper reckoned only yesterday what his victory would have ended — and the wait goes on: no Cleveland man has taken the rookie prize since Sandy Alomar in 1990, a vigil still second only to San Diego's. Boston's Payton Tolle finished third at 54 points on the strength of a dozen third-place votes. The two winners, both All-Stars this past summer, took the news in their hometowns at watch parties of roughly 70 friends and family apiece — which seems, for two men honored above all for showing up, exactly the right size of crowd.34

THE DUGOUT DESK: TONIGHT THE WRITERS JUDGE THE MEN AT THE WHEEL — MURPHY BIDS FOR A THIRD CROWN RUNNING, WHICH NONE HAS EVER WORN, AGAINST TWO APRIL INHERITORS, THE PALE HOSE'S RESURRECTIONIST AND THE PILOT OF THE EIGHT-AND-NINETY-WIN RAYS

The week's second sitting convenes this evening, when the writers read their Managers of the Year, and the six names on the bill share almost nothing but October: five were not finalists a year ago, and two were not even in their chairs on Opening Day. The ballots, as with the rookies', closed with the regular season, so no pennant and no champagne weighs in the scale.5

The American League offers three varieties of surprise. Kevin Cash's Rays were projected by the figuring house FanGraphs, on Opening Day itself, to finish 79-83 with about a one-in-four chance of October; they finished 98-64, took the East by four and a half games, and seeded first in their league — the longest-tenured manager in the game, twice honored already, making the familiar look miraculous on one of the game's thinnest payrolls. Chad Tracy was managing at Worcester on the 25th of April when Boston called; the club he inherited sat at 32-46 as late as the 25th of June, worst in the league by winning fraction, whereupon it ran off 32 wins in 37 games — a conflagration the town likened to Morgan's Magic of 1988, lit by another interim man — and went 55-29 down the stretch, the interim tag traded for a three-year contract in September. The father-and-son particular, should Tracy win, stands as yesterday's columns set it down. And Will Venable's White Sox, losers of a hundred games three seasons running and of a modern-record 121 as lately as 2024, won 84, took the league's sixth seed, swept Houston in the Wild Card round, and banked the franchise's first postseason series victory since the championship autumn of 2005.5

The National League's argument is between repetition and rescue. Pat Murphy, whose Brewers set a franchise record with 103 victories and led all the game for a second year running — this against projections of 81-odd wins, with 80 starts given to rookies, the most anywhere — bids to become the first man ever to take the award three years in succession; only four have ever won it twice running. Against him stand Don Mattingly, who inherited Philadelphia at 9-19 in late April and steered it to the fourth-best record in baseball thereafter and a fifth consecutive October; and Walt Weiss, whose first Atlanta season survived the springtime loss of four starting pitchers and a 162-game suspension besides, led the East from the 8th of April to the last day, and produced the franchise's seventh division flag in nine years — a campaign whose tone was set, the club's chroniclers insist, on the 7th of April, when the 62-year-old manager personally brought down Jorge Soler in a bench-clearing affray and his men answered with a 20-6 stretch. The Herald does not handicap the writers; it observes only that the evening must disappoint at least five clubhouses that have little else to regret.5

THE EXCHANGE DESK: THE WINTER'S SWEEPSTAKES OPENS ON THE MAN DETROIT COULD NOT KEEP — THE CORRIDORS AT LAS VEGAS MAKE THE FLUSHING NINE THE FAVORITES FOR SKUBAL, THE DODGERS WEIGH THEIR OWN SUMMER RENTAL, AND THE CHAMPIONS WAIT ON BAUERS' ANSWER

The General Managers Meetings opened in earnest at the Aria hotel Monday, the thirty front offices and the agents who farm them filing into the same corridors this paper mapped yesterday morning, and the talk has organized itself around a single left arm. Tarik Skubal — twice the American League's Cy Young man, dealt away at midseason by a sinking Detroit club in the very year its rookie infielder took the league's laurels, as the columns above attest4 — is expected to command the largest pitching contract in the history of the game, past the $325 million mark Yoshinobu Yamamoto presently holds. He turns 30 on the 20th of this month, and the question of how many years a prudent house gives a great arm with a surgical history is the question of the winter.6

The industry has already picked its favorite. "If the Mets want him, he's going to be a Met," one American League executive put it — the Flushing club having missed October two years running, with an owner of famous purse and a baseball-operations chief, David Stearns, whose whole career has preferred pitchers on short leashes; which appetite prevails will tell the tale. The Dodgers, who paid three prospects for Skubal's summer services, hear from rival quarters that they want hitting, not another arm — "The Dodgers need bats, not another arm," one executive said flatly, counting the grey in a lineup whose regulars run heavily past 30 — while the Blue Jays, who have lately bid on every great name and signed a $500 million extension besides, are nobody's afterthought, with the free outfielder Seiya Suzuki reckoned a natural fit for their order in any case. The Yankees, for once, are expected to sit the auction out: "I would be shocked if the Yankees made a real play for Skubal," a rival executive said, their wants running instead to second base, third base and a right-handed catcher, with the posted Japanese slugger Teruaki Sato — whose crossing the Far Pacific columns noted Sunday — a candidate for the Bronx corner.6

The champions, meanwhile, wait on a single signature. Milwaukee's winter hinges on whether Jake Bauers accepts his $23.15 million qualifying offer, an answer due with all the rest on the 17th, seven mornings hence; decline it and first base opens, accept it and the budget tightens. The harder arithmetic sits behind the plate: William Contreras, Most Valuable of the late World's Series, is now one season from the open market, and the front office that has made a practice of trading its stars a year early — the reader recalls Corbin Burnes — will at the least answer the telephone. All of it runs ahead of the same weather: the collective agreement has 21 mornings to live, and the trade expects a November of unusual commerce for exactly the reason Monday's columns gave — the last such winter signed away nearly a thousand millions before the freeze.6

THE ALMANAC DESK: THE CATCH IS GOING TO THE MAILS — MAYS IS NAMED THE FIFTIETH SUBJECT OF THE POST'S BLACK HERITAGE STAMPS, HIS BACK TO THE PLATE AND THE BALL DESCENDING, WITH SUMMITT OF THE LADY VOLS HONORED BESIDE HIM

The republic's mail will carry the game's finest outfielder. The United States Postal Service announced Monday that Willie Mays will be honored with a stamp in 2027, the fiftieth in its Black Heritage series, and the design chooses the one image that needs no caption: alongside the portrait runs the over-the-shoulder catch from the first game of the 1954 World's Series — back to the plate, glove out ahead of him in deepest center field, the New York Giants on their way to the title.7

The ledger beneath the picture is read from memory in most households: 22 seasons with the Giants of New York and San Francisco and the Mets at the close, two Most Valuable awards, a dozen Gold Gloves, and a manner of playing the game that made grown writers reach for their best adjectives for half a century. Mays died in 2024 at 93; the stamp arrives three years after the man departed, which is quick work as immortality goes.7

He travels in worthy company. The same announcement sets Pat Summitt upon a stamp of her own — the Tennessee basketball general who won 1,098 games and eight national championships for the Lady Vols before illness closed her bench in 2012, her portrait drawn after the cover of her book Reach for the Summit. The Herald's jurisdiction ends at the foul lines, but it knows a kindred record of showing up when it sees one, and it notes with satisfaction that a letter may soon travel under the two of them together. Some afternoons the mail will be worth watching for.7

A Tuesday with silver already on the table and more promised by nightfall. The rookies' prizes are bestowed, one to Detroit and one to Cincinnati, and the first item of the week's long bill is thereby discharged; the writers judge the managers this evening; Wednesday doubles the docket, the Cy Youngs and the writers' first reliever's prize read while the league stages its own awards theater at Las Vegas; and the Most Valuable verdicts close the books Thursday — the same day the courtroom at Brooklyn resumes, as Monday's columns noted. The forward ledger, ruled open before a word was set as the house requires, stands unmoved: nothing on the card before the spring exhibitions of Friday, the 19th of February, 101 mornings from this one, with Opening Night 134 mornings off on Wednesday, the 24th of March.1 The 17th keeps its double appointment seven mornings hence — qualifying answers and silver bats together — and the collective agreement has 21 mornings left to live, a figure the corridors of the Aria recite more fluently than any batting average. Until the morrow's dispatch, keep your scorecards near and your enthusiasms nearer.

~ THE HERALD ~

entry.title: Hot Stove Edition — the Ninth of November, Two Thousand and Twenty-Six
entry.content:
Is it spring training yet? Not yet — 135 days until Opening Night of the 2027 season — the first pitch of the new campaign, the clubs yet to be named.

THE MORNING HORSEHIDE HERALD

"Every Score Set Down, No Deed Unsung"

~ Being a Faithful Daily Chronicle of the National Pastime ~

Volume I · No. 124 · Monday, the Ninth of November, Two Thousand and Twenty-Six

No contests this day; the hot stove burns bright.

135 days until Opening Night of the 2027 season — the first pitch of the new campaign, the clubs yet to be named (Wednesday, the 24th of March, 2027).

News Around the League

THE NURSERY DESK: THE SENIOR CIRCUIT'S PUPILS TAKE THE FALL STARS BY SEVEN RUNS TO FOUR — CONFIDAN OF THE RED STOCKINGS' NURSERY CARRIES OFF THE MEDAL, SUSANA OPENS THE EVENING AT THREE-AND-A-HUNDRED MILES AN HOUR, AND THE DECIDING RUN COMES HOME BY A LOST ART, THE SQUEEZE

The hardest-hitting young man in the desert now owns the hardware to match. Yerlin Confidan, an outfielder in the Reds' nursery who has spent the autumn striking balls harder than anyone in the developmental circuit, doubled, drew a bases-loaded walk, and was named Most Valuable of the twentieth annual Fall Stars Game on Sunday night at Salt River Fields at Talking Stick, his National League pupils prevailing over the junior circuit's by 7-4 — the showcase, ten of the game's hundred best prospects on the card, that this paper billed only yesterday morning.2

The radar did the early talking. Jarlin Susana, the Washingtons' right-hander and the Fall League's hardest thrower, opened the game with fastballs of 102.7 and 103.1 mph and finished off Zion Rose — the Royals' outfielder taken sixth overall in the summer's draft — with an 88 mph sweeper, averaging 101.2 mph through a scoreless first inning.2 Kyle DeBarge of the North Stars was the bat of the evening, 2-for-2 with a double, a walk, two runs and two stolen bases, his 104.2 mph single the hardest-struck ball of the night; in the fifth he manufactured a run entirely alone, doubling off the Dodgers' left-hander Luke Fox and breaking for third with a jump so ambitious that the pitcher simply threw the ball away.2 Welbyn Francisca, the Cleveland infielder who leads the league's hitters at .419, added two of the finest defensive plays of the night at shortstop for good measure.2

Fox, to his credit, gathered himself after the DeBarge misadventure and struck out the side — the last of his victims, caught looking at a 93.4 mph four-seamer, being Aaron Parker of the Blue Jays, who had carried off the home-run derby's crown only the night before, as these columns recorded yesterday. The decision came in the eighth: Kevin Bazzell, a Washington catcher who had just erased a base-stealer with a throw of 1.86 seconds from mitt to bag, lined a 100.3 mph double, and Justin DeCriscio of the Mission nine brought him home by the lost art itself — a safety squeeze laid so gently on the grass before the plate that he beat it out for a single. The schoolhouse, the Herald is satisfied to report, remains in good order.2

THE LABOR DESK: 'DO NOT LOCK OUT BASEBALL' — MARTINEZ OF THE THREE CY YOUNGS, AMONG THE MOST PUNISHED MEN OF THE 1994 STOPPAGE, BIDS BOTH HOUSES FIGURE IT OUT FOR THE FANS WITH TWO-AND-TWENTY MORNINGS LEFT ON THE AGREEMENT

Pedro Martinez chose the tenth annual gala of his own foundation, at Boston on Saturday, to say what the sport's two houses have spent the autumn not saying to each other. "I feel for the fans, and I know when it's good, and it's good, baseball is good right now," the Hall of Famer said, by the account of Boston's own Herald — a paper of kindred name and, on this evidence, sound judgment in whom it quotes. "So stop the crap around and get something done and don't lock out baseball for the fans." He owned to being, honestly speaking, pissed — the word is his, and this desk prints it with the century's pardon — and he addressed the appeal to both sides of the table: "Please, for the fans, both sides, figure it out, a good way to get it done, and do not lock out baseball."3

Few men living are better credentialed to give the warning. When the strike of 1994 stopped the season, Martinez was a young arm on a Montreal club that owned the best record in baseball at 74-40 and dreams of a championship that died with the schedule — and the same cancellation left him a single day short of arbitration eligibility, so that the wage his talent had earned waited another year on the calendar's cruelty. "I was one of the most punished players at that moment because I had talent, and I needed to wait until arbitration to make my money," he said. "I might be insignificant, but I lived it before. I experienced that before."3

The calendar he addresses is not a sentimental one: the collective agreement dies on the 1st of December — 22 mornings from this one — with the owners' latest offer, tendered Tuesday last, proposing to delay their salary cap's arrival to 2028 rather than to withdraw it, and the union standing where it has stood throughout. "Back then, there was a need for other things to change, and they changed for the better," Martinez said of 1994. "This time, there's no excuse." The Herald's sympathies on matters of the purse are of long record and want no restating here; it observes only that when a man with three Cy Young trophies and a plaque at Cooperstown says the fans do not deserve to be mistreated, both houses might profitably take the afternoon to listen.3

THE LAURELS DESK: FIVE NIGHTS OF HARDWARE BEGIN WITH THE ROOKIES THIS EVENING — MESSICK'S CANDIDACY CARRIES A SIX-AND-THIRTY-YEAR CLEVELAND DROUGHT, THE WRITERS VOTE A RELIEVER'S PRIZE FOR THE FIRST TIME, AND THE HERALD REMINDS THE READER THAT POLLS ARE POLLS

The silverware season proper opens tonight. The writers' association reads its Rookie of the Year verdicts this evening at 7 o'clock Eastern on the MLB Network — the first of the week's awards, long marked on this paper's calendar. The Managers of the Year follow Tuesday; Wednesday doubles the bill, the Cy Youngs and the writers' new Reliever of the Year prizes read that night while the league stages its own MLB Awards from the Chelsea Theater at the Cosmopolitan of Las Vegas, the Hank Aaron awards, the Rivera and Hoffman reliever medals, the Comeback men and the All-MLB teams among the honors, with the comedian Roy Wood Jr. and Mookie Betts holding the gavels; and the Most Valuable verdicts close the week Thursday.4

Tonight's business first. The National League's rookie case lies among three: JJ Wetherholt of the Mound City nine, whose glove at second base banked 25 outs above average; Carson Benge, the Mets' outfielder, 20 home runs and the most balanced ledger of the trio; and Sal Stewart of the Cincinnatis, whose 112 runs driven in stood third in all the game. The American League's is a two-man argument of the everyday against the every-fifth-day: Detroit's Kevin McGonigle and his .806 on-base-plus-slugging against Cleveland's Parker Messick, who threw 186 and one-third innings to a 2.56 earned-run average — work good enough that he stands among the Cy Young finalists besides, only the sixth rookie ever to finish in that balloting's top three, after Skenes, Fernández, Gooden, Valenzuela and Fidrych. Should Messick prevail tonight, he ends the second-longest rookie drought in the game: no Cleveland man has taken the award since Sandy Alomar in 1990, a wait exceeded only by San Diego's, running since Benito Santiago in 1987.4

The week's other arguments, with the Herald's standing rule beside them. MLB.com's final staff poll of late September made Pete Crow-Armstrong its unanimous choice for the National League's Most Valuable — all 38 first-place votes — and made Misiorowski and Schlittler its unanimous choices for the two Cy Youngs; a poll is a poll, its sponsor is named, and the trophies themselves are decided by the ballot alone, which is read this week and not before. Among the managers, Pat Murphy, lately champion of the world, seeks a third Manager of the Year in succession, while opposite him stand two mid-season inheritors: Don Mattingly, under whom the Phillies played to the fourth-best record in the game after a 9-19 beginning, and Chad Tracy, who steadied the Boston club to its Wild Card berth — and who, should he win, makes the Tracys, father Jim and son Chad, the first father and son ever to take any of the writers' awards. The writers vote a reliever's prize for the first time this year besides; whether their electors and the panel of old relievers who award the Rivera and Hoffman medals can agree on the same arms Wednesday night is precisely the sort of question the Herald keeps its subscriptions for.4

THE EXCHANGE DESK: THE THIRTY FRONT OFFICES REPAIR TO THE DESERT WITH NINESCORE FREE AGENTS AND MORE ON THE BOOKS — THE GENERAL MANAGERS CONVENE AT LAS VEGAS UNDER THE LOCKOUT'S SHADOW, MINDFUL THAT THE LAST SUCH NOVEMBER SIGNED AWAY NEARLY A THOUSAND MILLIONS BEFORE THE FREEZE

The winter's commerce takes a roof this week: executives of all thirty clubs gather at the Aria hotel of Las Vegas for the annual General Managers Meetings — the convening these columns flagged twice last week — with more than 180 free agents on the open market and the agents who represent them working the same corridors, a convenience the telephone winter never affords. The business sits under one long shadow. With the collective agreement expiring December 1, the trade braces for a November of unusual urgency, and the precedent is exactly five winters old: in 2021, with a lockout looming, Seager signed for ten years and $325 million, Semien for seven years and $175 million, Báez for six and $140 million, and the pitchers Scherzer, Ray and Gausman for nine figures apiece — six men and $995 million subscribed before the freeze came down, with eight more at $50 million or better in the same scramble.5

The welcome wagon carries names the Herald's readers met only this past week. Randy Flores, whose removal from St. Louis to the head of Houston's baseball operations these columns have chronicled, attends his first meetings in that chair, as does Taylor Smith, late of the Rays and the Red Sox, now atop the Athletics' operation; among the second chairs come Rob Cerfolio, promoted at St. Louis only Friday as Saturday's columns told, Cam Castro, the Athletics' new general manager out of the champions' development rooms, and Jared Banner of the Orioles, while Anirudh Kilambi of the Washingtons attends his first such meetings in the general manager's office he has held since last December.5

What the corridors will deal in is talk, and the talk has its favorite names. The Gulf Coast club will be asked all week about Drew Rasmussen, whose $20 million wage for next season would be the largest in the franchise's books — the baseball operations chief Erik Neander professes "every intention" of keeping his ace, which is what a man says in either case. Seattle's Dipoto, never bashful in the market, holds a stocked rotation and a bare cupboard of hitting, so the names of Kirby and Hancock will circulate; Abrams of the Capital nine, Marte of the Desert nine, Kwan of the Lake Erie men and Peña of the Houston nine will all be spoken of, chiefly by men who do not employ them. And the eight qualifying-offer men — Arozarena, Lowe, Suzuki, Rogers, Bauers, Morejon, Jeffers and Bednar — have until the 17th at 4 o'clock Eastern to answer their $23.15 million tenders. The industry's consensus holds that all eight decline, and history leans the same way: of the 165 men ever tendered the offer, just 18 have accepted — though the reader will note, as the agents surely do, that four of those 18 came only last winter.5

THE PANTHEON DESK: EIGHT NAMES WAIT ON SIXTEEN VOTES — THE CONTEMPORARY ERA PANEL TAKES UP BILL WHITE, FIRST BASEMAN, BROADCASTER AND PRESIDENT OF THE NATIONAL LEAGUE, WITH ITS VERDICT SET FOR THE SIXTH OF DECEMBER

The Hall of Fame's winter docket has opened its first argument. The Contemporary Baseball Era committee — the panel of 16 that weighs managers, executives and umpires — reads its results on Sunday, the 6th of December, with eight candidates on its ballot, and the columnist Anthony Castrovince spent Sunday making the case for the most varied life among the eight: Bill White, now 92, whom Cooperstown honored only last summer with the Buck O'Neil Award, a distinction seven people in all have held, for his impact on the game beyond its box scores. O'Neil himself received that honor in 2008 and his plaque in the gallery posthumously in 2022; White's partisans would prefer to see the order reversed.6

The case wants no padding, only addition. The player: thirteen seasons, a .286 average, 1,706 hits and 202 home runs, eight All-Star selections, seven consecutive Gold Gloves at first base, third in the Most Valuable balloting of 1964 and a champion that same October with the Cardinals. The broadcaster: the first Black play-by-play man ever engaged by a major-league club, hired to the Yankee air in 1971 and seated beside Phil Rizzuto for the better part of eighteen seasons, his call of Bucky Dent's home run in the playoff of 1978 among the catalogue's treasures. The executive: five years as president of the National League from 1989, the man in the chair when the league added the Marlins and the Rockies in 1993. And the road beneath it all: signed out of Hiram College by the Giants in 1953, the second Black player in the Carolina League, the desegregator of several minor-league clubs, and nearly two years in the Army besides.6

No single line of the ledger, Castrovince allows, carries Cooperstown by itself; the argument is the totality — a professional life touching parts of five decades, each room entered first or nearly first, and the door held open behind him. "Bill had no choice but to accept that job," his old teammate Bob Gibson once said of the league presidency. "Not for himself but for other people." White's own accounting was always simpler: "I demanded to be recognized for what I accomplished. Nothing more." The Herald, which keeps a standing affection for men who did several jobs well in an age that prefers one job done loudly, will have the panel's answer on the first Sunday of December.6

A Monday that opens the winter's busiest week. The writers read their first verdicts this evening — the rookies, as foretold — with the managers Tuesday, the Cy Youngs Wednesday and the Most Valuable men Thursday; the thirty front offices convene meanwhile at Las Vegas, where the league also stages its Wednesday awards theater, so that Nevada holds very nearly the whole apparatus of the game this week; and the courtroom at Brooklyn resumes its own proceedings Thursday, as Sunday's columns noted. The forward ledger, ruled open at first light as the house requires, stands unmoved: nothing on the card before the spring exhibitions of Friday, the 19th of February, 102 mornings from this one, with Opening Night 135 mornings off on Wednesday, the 24th of March.1 The 17th keeps its double appointment eight mornings hence — qualifying answers and silver bats together — the Hall's Contemporary Era panel reports on the 6th of December, and the collective agreement has 22 mornings left to live, a circumstance on which the week's plainest sermon was preached Saturday at Boston, gratis, by a man with three Cy Young trophies. Until the morrow's dispatch, keep your scorecards near and your enthusiasms nearer.

entry.title: Hot Stove Edition — the Eighth of November, Two Thousand and Twenty-Six
entry.content:
Is it spring training yet? Not yet — 136 days until Opening Night of the 2027 season — the first pitch of the new campaign, the clubs yet to be named.

THE MORNING HORSEHIDE HERALD

"Every Score Set Down, No Deed Unsung"

~ Being a Faithful Daily Chronicle of the National Pastime ~

Volume I · No. 123 · Sunday, the Eighth of November, Two Thousand and Twenty-Six

No contests this day; the hot stove burns bright.

136 days until Opening Night of the 2027 season — the first pitch of the new campaign, the clubs yet to be named (Wednesday, the 24th of March, 2027).

News Around the League

THE NURSERY DESK: THE UNDERSTUDY STEALS THE SHOW — PARKER OF THE TORONTO SCHOOLING, HANDED A DERBY INVITATION ON SHORT NOTICE, OUT-SLUGS THE AUTUMN FIELD WITH NINETEEN CIRCUIT CLOUTS AND CARRIES THE CROWN TO THE CATCHERS' ROOM

The Arizona Fall League's home-run derby, which these columns flagged Thursday among the week's appointments, went off Saturday night and handed its trophy to a man who was not on the original bill. Aaron Parker, a catcher of 23 in the Blue Jays' system, entered the field as a late substitute for the Dodgers' young prospect Chase Harlan, drew the seventh position of the eight, and proceeded to out-hit every invited guest: he led all entrants with 19 home runs in sum and beat the Cardinals' prospect Tai Peete in the final round by a count of 2 to 1.2

The power is no rumor newly minted. Parker struck a career-best 19 home runs this season — his first campaign of double figures as a professional, and precisely the number, the reader will smile to note, that he totaled across Saturday's rounds — and his autumn work for Mesa includes a drive measured at 451 feet.2 He joins a short and instructive roll of derby champions: the Pirates' giant Tony Blanco Jr. took last year's edition with an exhibition the desert still talks about, one ball leaving his bat at 122.9 mph.2

The main event follows directly: the Fall Stars Game, the autumn circuit's twentieth annual showcase, convenes this very evening at Salt River Fields at Talking Stick, 8 o'clock Eastern, with ten of the game's hundred best prospects on the two rosters and the Rangers' shortstop Sebastian Walcott at the head of the bill — the particulars as this paper laid them out Thursday.3 The nursery columns remind the reader why the exhibition earns its ink: last November's Fall Stars leadoff man was Kevin McGonigle, who spent this past week as a finalist for the Rookie of the Year.3

THE CHRISTENING DESK: BEFORE YOU ARE A YANKEE, YOU ARE A HIGHLANDER — THE BRONX MEN'S TOP FARM CLUB REACHES BACK TO 1903 FOR ITS NEW NAME, AND THE DEADBALL DESK PRONOUNCES IT THE WINTER'S FINEST SIGNING

A piece of news after this paper's own heart arrived Saturday from the anthracite country of Pennsylvania: the Yankees' Triple-A club, these fourteen seasons the Scranton/Wilkes-Barre RailRiders, has rechristened itself the Scranton/Wilkes-Barre Highlanders — the very name the parent franchise wore from 1903, when it came north from Baltimore, through 1912, in honor of its ballpark's perch on the high ground of upper Manhattan. "Before they were the Yankees, they were the Highlanders," said the club president Sean Reilly. "And now, once again, before you're a Yankee, you're a Highlander."4 The desk that still sets its type by the standards of that era declares the sentiment unimprovable.

The announcement was made a festival: an all-day affair at PNC Field with food trucks, live music and a drone show, the proceedings carried live on the Yankees' own network with the broadcaster Michael Kay as master of ceremonies, and the Yankee grandee Tino Martinez and the sometime manager Joe Maddon — a son of nearby Hazleton — among the guests. Highlanders is the fourth identity in the franchise's books, after the Red Barons of 1989 through 2006 (a Phillies affiliate in those days), the plain Yankees of 2007 through 2012, and the RailRiders since; the coming season is the club's twentieth as the Bronx men's top farm.4

The new livery splits its loyalties agreeably between the mountains and the Bronx. The primary mark is a bear in hiking kit shouldering a bat beneath a pinstriped sky — an homage, the club allows, to a genuine bear occasionally sighted in the ballpark's parking lot — with a campfire of bat-logs among the secondary marks, all from the Louisville design house that drew the Hudson Valley Renegades' pinstriped heavens besides; the home uniforms keep pinstripes, a Yankees sleeve patch and an interlocking SWB. The mascot Champ, a bleacher creature by species, stays on. And the clerks note two fine prints: at 32 characters the Scranton/Wilkes-Barre Highlanders own the longest name in professional baseball, and the club plays in neither Scranton nor Wilkes-Barre but in the town of Moosic. The Highlanders take the field March 26 against the Worcester Red Sox, with the home opener set for April 6.4

THE FAR PACIFIC DESK: A GUARDIAN OF THE OTHER OCEAN PUTS TO SEA — TSENG OF THE FIVE-AND-TWENTY SAVES IS POSTED FROM TAIWAN, HIS WINDOW OPEN THIS VERY MORNING AND SHUT TWO DAYS BEFORE CHRISTMAS, IF THE LOCKOUT DOES NOT SHUT IT FIRST

A week to the day since Teruaki Sato weighed anchor, the autumn's eastward traffic gains another vessel. Jyun-Yue Tseng, right-handed closer of Taiwan's Fubon Guardians — no kin to the Cleveland club of that name, whose November is passing in a Brooklyn courtroom elsewhere in these columns — is entering the posting system, and the thirty clubs may treat with him from this very Sunday until December 22.5

The ledger travels well. Tseng is 25, and this season in the Chinese Professional Baseball League he went 5-3 with 25 saves across 48 games, striking out 65 men against 13 walks in 52 and one-third innings. The international stage has seen him twice: in this year's World Baseball Classic he threw hitless innings against South Korea and the Czech Republic and banked a save, his four-seam fastball averaging 93.7 mph against the Koreans with a cutter alongside. The résumé runs back further than most — he pitched in the Little League World Series of 2014, and was the CPBL's Rookie of the Year in 2021.5

The counting-house terms are the standard tariff — a signing club owes his Taiwan employers a posting fee starting at a fifth of the first 25 millions of any major-league contract — but the calendar is the clause to watch. The collective agreement dies on the 1st of December with a lockout widely expected, and the freeze may cut Tseng's negotiating window short by three weeks; the winter's every transaction now runs ahead of that same weather, as the Herald's labor columns have had steady occasion to observe.5

THE COURTROOM DESK: 'THERE WAS NO MORE INFORMATION LIKE THAT' — A COOPERATING BETTOR SAYS THE INSIDE WORD ON CLASE'S PITCHES DRIED UP WHEN THE MIZUHARA SCANDAL BROKE, AND THE WEEK'S TESTIMONY CLOSES ON THE QUESTION OF THE CHICKENS

The pitch-rigging trial of Emmanuel Clase and Luis Ortiz, whose Thursday session these columns reported Friday, closed its week with the testimony of Luis de Aza Baez, a cooperating government witness who told the Brooklyn jury he placed dozens of bets and won thousands of dollars on the velocity of selected Clase pitches in 2023 "because I had inside information." The word came never from Clase himself, he said, but from Enoc Pena, an associate of the pitcher's, often through a group chat titled "Uber Inc." — its members, like the witness, ride-share drivers in Massachusetts at the time. De Aza Baez opened a betting account in his wife's name to raise his limits and folded the pitch wagers into parlays to fatten the payouts.6

The detail that lifts the day's testimony into the historical record is where the well ran dry. When he asked for more such information in 2024, De Aza Baez testified, he was told that because of "what was going on with Ohtani, there was no more information like that" — the season the sporting world learned that millions had moved from Shohei Ohtani's bank account to an illegal bookmaking operation, a theft of nearly 17 millions to which the interpreter Ippei Mizuhara later pleaded guilty and for which he now sits in prison, Ohtani himself cleared of all wrongdoing. One scandal's scrutiny, by this account, starved another.6

The jury was also shown a text message Clase is alleged to have sent Pena on September 30, 2023, speaking of "killing the first two chickens" — instructions, the witness said, to bet on a Clase pitch to an inning's third batter, but only if the first two had been retired; Clase did not appear in that day's game, and the defense maintains that roosters and chickens in such messages often referred to cockfighting, a legal pastime in the Dominican Republic. De Aza Baez acknowledged he will forfeit $69,000 in winnings and testify truthfully in exchange for the government dropping a wire-fraud charge against him. "This is a case about big talk and small bets," said Todd Spodek, counsel to the co-defendant Robinson Vásquez Germosen, after the session. The proceedings resume Thursday; the Herald's practice is unchanged — the allegations are reported as allegations, and the verdict is left to the jury.6

THE INFIRMARY WARD AND THE INK DESK: CARROLL OF THE SONORAN NINE HAS HIS ELBOW SWEPT CLEAN AND IS PROMISED FOR THE SPRING — THE METROPOLITANS KEEP THEIR MENDED WANDERER STOCK FOR ANOTHER YEAR, AND STITCH A SLEEVE FOR KOOSMAN

From the desert comes news of a tidying rather than a repair: Corbin Carroll underwent surgery this week to remove loose bodies from his right elbow, the Diamondbacks confirming the operation Friday, with full recovery reckoned at about eight weeks — which lands him in the new year with a month and more to spare before the first exhibitions of February 19.71 The season behind him was a catalogue of endurance: a .239 average with 22 home runs, 78 runs driven in, 33 doubles and 17 three-base hits — the most in his league — compiled around a hamate operation that cost him most of the spring and a back that nagged him through the second half. Carroll is 26, a three-time All-Star, the National League's Rookie of the Year of 2023, and the holder, since the month's turn, of the first Gold Glove of his career in right field, as these columns recorded when Rawlings read its verdicts.7

In Queens, the ink desk logs a smaller but sweeter signature: the Mets have re-signed the right-hander Robert Stock, who turns 37 this month, to a one-year contract. Stock's 2026 ran to seven starts and a relief turn — 1-3, with a 5.93 earned-run average over 30 and one-third innings — but it held one evening worth the whole ledger: on August 31 at Tampa Bay he threw five and one-third scoreless innings in a 3-2 decision, his first big-league victory since 2019. Numbness in his fingers, a souvenir of March surgery for thoracic outlet syndrome, shelved him in mid-September; the man has pitched for eight big-league organizations, in South Korea and Mexico, and for the independent Long Island Ducks, and his persistence has now out-lasted the ailment's patience.8

The same club sewed a graver stitch: the Mets announced Thursday that their 2027 uniforms will carry a memorial sleeve patch for Jerry Koosman, the left arm of the Miracle Mets, who died a week ago this morning at 83 and for whom this paper lowered its colors on Monday last.8 The patch is a small thing as cloth goes; the memory it rides on is not.

The Sabbath's ledger runs lighter than the week's and none the worse for it: a derby won by an understudy, a christening in the anthracite country that this desk will be savoring for days, a new sail on the Pacific horizon, and a courtroom gone quiet until Thursday. The forward ledger, ruled open before a word of this was set, stands exactly where Saturday left it — nothing on the card before the spring exhibitions of Friday, the 19th of February, 103 mornings distant, with Opening Night 136 mornings off on Wednesday, the 24th of March.1 Nearer at hand the week fills to the brim: the Fall Stars convene at Salt River Fields this very evening;3 the writers begin reading their award verdicts on the morrow, the rookies summoned first and the Most Valuable men to follow Thursday; the general managers convene at Las Vegas in the week now opening, as these columns noted Thursday; the 17th keeps its double appointment, qualifying answers and silver bats alike, nine mornings hence; and the collective agreement has 23 mornings left to live. Until the morrow's dispatch, keep your scorecards near and your enthusiasms nearer.

~ THE HERALD ~
